lessons.title: Stripped of Everything, Something Remains
lessons.key_idea: When Frankl lost his home, family, work and even his name in the camps, he discovered that a person's inner life cannot be fully taken away.

lessons.title: Shock, Numbness and the Mind's Defenses
lessons.key_idea: Frankl observed that prisoners moved through stages of shock, apathy and disoriented release, and that the numbness was a way to protect the mind.
issues: scene 1: Each stage box has a small stray navy dot near its right edge (beside the lightning bolt, at the end of the flatline, beside the question mark). In the Shock and Confusion boxes it has no meaning and reads as a leftover artifact. (fix: Remove the dots from the Shock and Confusion boxes. Keep a dot only on the Numbness flatline, and only if it is meant as the pulse endpoint.)

scene 7: The JOY bar is about 80% full. That contradicts the narration's 'feeling no joy at all' and the idea of slowly relearning how to feel. (fix: Show the bar nearly empty (about 10–15%), or animate it filling only slightly, so it reads as joy just beginning to return.)

scene 7: The person floats in mid-air above the flowers, well above the ground line, so they do not read as walking through the meadow. (fix: Lower the figure so it stands on the ground line among the flowers, with the flowers in front of or around it.)

lessons.title: The Last Human Freedom
lessons.key_idea: Even when every outside freedom is gone, we keep the freedom to choose our attitude toward what happens to us.

lessons.title: Love Reaches Beyond the Barbed Wire
lessons.key_idea: Frankl found strength by picturing his wife, which showed him that love can sustain a person even across distance and uncertainty.

lessons.title: A Why to Live For
lessons.key_idea: Prisoners who held on to a future purpose, like a person waiting or a task to finish, endured better than those who lost hope.

lessons.title: Three Paths to Meaning
lessons.key_idea: Frankl's logotherapy says we find meaning by creating or doing something, by loving or experiencing something, and by how we face unavoidable suffering.

lessons.title: Life Is Asking You
lessons.key_idea: Instead of asking what we want from life, Frankl urges us to answer what life is asking of us, turning even pain into a meaningful response.
issues: scene 6: A stray slanted line leans against the doctor figure's shoulder and reaches the floor. It reads as a broken artifact, not as a recognizable cane or chair, so the drawing looks unclear. (fix: Remove the slanted line or replace it with a clearly drawn chair or cane that does not touch the figure. Seat the doctor visibly on a chair facing the empty chair.)

scene 7: Four scattered indigo dots float between the shield and the right-hand panel. They illustrate nothing in the narration and look like leftover particles. They also crowd the left group into the right group. (fix: Remove the dots, or replace them with a clear connector, such as an arrow from the shield to the 'His loss had not changed' text. Add spacing between the left and right groups.)

plan.title: Man's Search for Meaning
plan.author: Viktor E. Frankl
plan.confidence_note: I know this book's two parts in detail: Frankl's account of the camps and his outline of logotherapy, including the later postscript on tragic optimism.
plan.one_liner: A psychiatrist survives the Nazi camps and discovers what keeps a person going when everything is taken.
plan.summary: Viktor Frankl was a Viennese psychiatrist who spent years as a prisoner in Nazi concentration camps, including Auschwitz. In the first part of the book, he describes camp life from the inside. He traces how prisoners reacted in stages, from shock, to numbness, to the strange disorientation of liberation. He noticed that those who held on to a reason to live, such as a loved one, unfinished work, or a future goal, were often better able to endure. In the second part, Frankl explains logotherapy, his approach to psychology. He argues that our deepest drive is not pleasure or power but meaning. He says we can find it through what we create, through what and whom we love, and through the attitude we choose toward suffering we cannot avoid.
